Main.sentence: Black is a ___E:racial U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial)___ classification of people, usually a ___E:political U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Politics)___ and ___E:skin color U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_skin_color)___ -based category for specific populations with a mid- to dark brown ___E:complexion U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Complexion)___ .

Often in countries with socially based systems of ___E:racial classification U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_classification)___ in the ___E:Western world U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_world)___ , the term "black" is used to describe persons who are perceived as darker-skinned in contrast to other populations.

It is most commonly used for people of ___E:sub-Saharan African U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-Saharan_Africa)___ ancestry, ___E:Indigenous Australians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indigenous_Australians)___ , and ___E:Melanesians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Melanesians)___ , though it has been applied in many contexts to other groups, and is no indicator of any close ancestral relationship whatsoever.

However, not all people considered "black" have ___E:dark skin U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_skin)___ and often additional ___E:phenotypical U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Phenotype)___ characteristics are relevant, such as certain facial and hair-texture features.
Indigenous African societies do not use the term black as a racial identity outside of influences brought by Western cultures.

Contemporary ___E:anthropologists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthropologist)___ and other scientists, while recognizing the reality of biological variation between different human populations, regard the concept of a unified, distinguishable "Black race" as ___E:socially constructed U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_constructionism)___ .

Different societies apply different criteria regarding who is classified "black", and these social constructs have changed over time. In a number of countries, societal variables affect classification as much as skin color, and the social criteria for "blackness" vary. Some perceive the term 'black' as a derogatory, outdated, reductive or otherwise unrepresentative label, and as a result neither use nor define it, especially in African countries with little to no history of colonial ___E:racial segregation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_segregation)___ .
In the ___E:anglosphere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglosphere)___ , the term can carry a variety of meanings depending on the country.

While the term "person of color" is commonly used and accepted in the ___E:United States U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_States)___ ,  the near-sounding term " ___E:colored person U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colored)___ " is considered highly offensive, except in South Africa, where it is a descriptor for a person of ___E:mixed race U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiracial_people)___ .
In other regions such as ___E:Australasia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Australasia)___ , settlers applied the adjective "black" to the indigenous population.

It was universally regarded as highly offensive in Australia until the 1960s and 70s. "Black" was generally not used as a noun, but rather as an adjective qualifying some other descriptor (e.g. "black ****").
As desegregation progressed after the 1967 referendum, some Aboriginals adopted the term, following the American fashion, but it remains problematic.

Several American style guides,   including the AP Stylebook , changed their guides to capitalize the 'b' in 'black', following the 2020 ___E:murder of George Floyd U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Murder_of_George_Floyd)___ , an ___E:African American U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans)___ .
The ASA Style Guide says that the 'b' should not be capitalized.
Numerous communities of dark-skinned peoples are present in ___E:North Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Africa)___ , some dating from prehistoric communities.

Others descend from migrants via the historical ___E:trans-Saharan trade U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Saharan_trade)___ or, after the Arab invasions of North Africa in the 7th century, from slaves from the ___E:trans-Saharan slave trade U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trans-Saharan_slave_trade)___ in North Africa.

In the 18th century, the Moroccan Sultan ___E:Moulay Ismail U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moulay_Ismail)___ "the Warrior King" (1672–1727) raised a corps of 150,000 black soldiers, called his ___E:Black Guard U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Black_Guard)___ .

According to ___E:Carlos Moore U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Moore_(writer))___ , resident scholar at Brazil's University of the State of Bahia, in the 21st century Afro-multiracials in the ___E:Arab world U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arab_world)___ , including Arabs in North Africa, self-identify in ways that resemble multi-racials in ___E:Latin America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_America)___ .

He claims that darker-toned Arabs, much like darker-toned ___E:Latin Americans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Latin_Americans)___ , consider themselves ___E:white U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/White_people)___ because they have some distant white ancestry.

Egyptian President ___E:Anwar Sadat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anwar_Sadat)___ had a mother who was a dark-skinned ___E:Nubian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nubians)___ Sudanese ( ___E:Sudanese Arab U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudanese_Arabs)___ ) woman and a father who was a lighter-skinned ___E:Egyptian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Egyptians)___ .
In response to an advertisement for an acting position, as a young man he said, "I am not white but I am not exactly black either.
My blackness is tending to reddish".

Due to the ___E:patriarchal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patriarchy)___ nature of Arab society, Arab men, including during the slave trade in North Africa, enslaved more African women than men. The female slaves were often put to work in domestic service and agriculture.

The men interpreted the ___E:Quran U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quran)___ to permit sexual relations between a male master and his enslaved females outside of marriage (see ___E:Ma malakat aymanukum and sex U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ma_malakat_aymanukum_and_sex)___ ),   leading to many ___E:mixed-race U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed-race)___ children.
When an enslaved woman became pregnant with her Arab master's child, she was considered as umm walad or "mother of a child", a status that granted her privileged rights.
The child was given rights of inheritance to the father's property, so mixed-race children could share in any wealth of the father.
Because the society was ___E:patrilineal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrilineal)___ , the children inherited their fathers' social status at birth and were born free.

Some mixed-race children succeeded their respective fathers as rulers, such as Sultan ___E:Ahmad al-Mansur U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahmad_al-Mansur)___ , who ruled ___E:Morocco U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Morocco)___ from 1578 to 1608. He was not technically considered as a mixed-race child of a slave; his mother was ___E:Fulani U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fulani)___ and a ___E:concubine U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concubine)___ of his father.

In early 1991, non-Arabs of the ___E:Zaghawa people U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaghawa_people)___ of Sudan attested that they were victims of an intensifying Arab ___E:apartheid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid)___ campaign, segregating Arabs and non-Arabs (specifically, people of ___E:Nilotic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilotic_peoples)___ ancestry).
Sudanese Arabs, who controlled the government, were widely referred to as practicing apartheid against Sudan's non-Arab citizens.
The government was accused of "deftly manipulating Arab solidarity" to carry out policies of apartheid and ___E:ethnic cleansing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethnic_cleansing)___ .

___E:Sudanese Arabs U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudanese_Arabs)___ are also black people in that they are culturally and linguistically ___E:Arabized U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabization)___ indigenous peoples of ___E:Sudan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudan)___ of mostly ___E:Nilo-Saharan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilo-Saharan_languages)___ , ___E:Nubian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nubians)___ ,  and ___E:Cushitic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cushitic_languages)___  ancestry; their skin tone and appearance resembles that of other black people.

___E:American University U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_University)___ economist ___E:George Ayittey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Ayittey)___ accused the Arab government of Sudan of practicing acts of racism against black citizens.
According to Ayittey, "In Sudan... the Arabs monopolized power and excluded blacks – Arab apartheid."  Many African commentators joined Ayittey in accusing Sudan of practicing Arab apartheid.

In the ___E:Sahara U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahara)___ , the native ___E:Tuareg U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tuareg_people)___ ___E:Berber U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berbers)___ populations kept " ___E:negro U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negro)___ " slaves.

Most of these captives were of ___E:Nilo-Saharan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilo-Saharan_languages)___ extraction, and were either purchased by the Tuareg nobles from slave markets in the ___E:Western Sudan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudan_(region))___ or taken during raids.

Their origin is denoted via the ___E:Ahaggar Berber U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamahaq_language)___ word Ibenheren (sing. Ébenher ), which alludes to slaves that only spoke a ___E:Nilo-Saharan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilo-Saharan_languages)___ language.
These slaves were also sometimes known by the borrowed ___E:Songhay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Songhay_languages)___ term Bella .

Similarly, the ___E:Sahrawi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sahrawi_people)___ indigenous peoples of the ___E:Western Sahara U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Sahara)___ observed a class system consisting of high ___E:castes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caste)___ and low castes.
Outside of these traditional tribal boundaries were "Negro" slaves, who were drawn from the surrounding areas.

In ___E:Ethiopia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia)___ and ___E:Somalia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somalia)___ , the slave classes mainly consisted of captured peoples from the Sudanese-Ethiopian and Kenyan-Somali international borders  or other surrounding areas of ___E:Nilotic U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nilotic_peoples)___ and ___E:Bantu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Somali_Bantus)___ peoples who were collectively known as Shanqella  and Adone (both analogues to "negro" in an English-speaking context).
Some of these slaves were captured during territorial conflicts in the Horn of Africa and then sold off to slave merchants.
The earliest representation of this tradition dates from a seventh or eighth century BC inscription belonging to the ___E:Kingdom of Damat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/D%CA%BFmt)___ .

These captives and others of analogous morphology were distinguished as tsalim barya (dark-skinned slave) in contrast with the Afroasiatic-speaking nobles or saba qayh ("red men") or light-skinned slave; while on the other hand, western racial category standards do not differentiate between saba qayh ("red men"—light-skinned) or saba tiqur ("black men"—dark-skinned) Horn Africans (of either Afroasiatic-speaking, Nilotic-speaking or Bantu origin) thus considering all of them as "black people" (and in some case "negro") according to Western society's notion of race.

In ___E:South Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Africa)___ , the period of colonisation resulted in many unions and marriages between ___E:European U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_ethnic_groups)___ and Africans ( ___E:Bantu peoples of South Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantu_peoples_of_South_Africa)___ and ___E:Khoisans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khoisan)___ ) from various tribes, resulting in mixed-race children.

As the European ___E:colonialists U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colonialists)___ acquired control of territory, they generally pushed the mixed-race and African populations into second-class status.

During the first half of the 20th century, the white-dominated government classified the population according to four main racial groups: Black , White , Asian (mostly ___E:Indian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_South_Africans)___ ), and Coloured .

The Coloured group included people of mixed Bantu, Khoisan, and European ancestry (with some ___E:Malay U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Malays)___ ancestry, especially in the ___E:Western Cape U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Western_Cape)___ ).
The Coloured definition occupied an intermediary political position between the Black and White definitions in South Africa.
It imposed a system of legal racial segregation, a complex of laws known as ___E:apartheid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/History_of_South_Africa_in_the_apartheid_era)___ .

The ___E:apartheid U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Apartheid)___ bureaucracy devised complex (and often arbitrary) criteria in the ___E:Population Registration Act U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_Registration_Act)___ of 1945 to determine who belonged in which group.
Minor officials administered tests to enforce the classifications.

When it was unclear from a person's physical appearance whether the individual should be considered Coloured or Black, the " ___E:pencil test U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pencil_test_(South_Africa))___ " was used. A pencil was inserted into a person's hair to determine if the hair was kinky enough to hold the pencil, rather than having it pass through, as it would with smoother hair. If so, the person was classified as Black.
Such classifications sometimes divided families.

___E:Sandra Laing U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sandra_Laing)___ is a South African woman who was classified as Coloured by authorities during the apartheid era, due to her ___E:skin colour U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_skin_colour)___ and ___E:hair texture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hair#Texture)___ , although her parents could prove at least three generations of European ancestors.
At age 10, she was expelled from her all-white school.
The officials' decisions based on her anomalous appearance disrupted her family and adult life. She was the subject of the 2008 biographical dramatic film Skin , which won numerous awards.
During the apartheid era, those classed as "Coloured" were oppressed and discriminated against.
But, they had limited rights and overall had slightly better socioeconomic conditions than those classed as "Black".
The government required that Blacks and Coloureds live in areas separate from Whites, creating large townships located away from the cities as areas for Blacks.
In the post-apartheid era, the Constitution of South Africa has declared the country to be a "Non-racial democracy".

In an effort to redress past injustices, the ANC government has introduced laws in support of ___E:affirmative action U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affirmative_action)___ policies for Blacks; under these they define "Black" people to include "Africans", "Coloureds" and "Asians".
Some ___E:affirmative action U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Affirmative_action)___ policies favor "Africans" over "Coloureds" in terms of qualifying for certain benefits.

Some South Africans categorized as "African Black" say that "Coloureds" did not suffer as much as they did during apartheid. "Coloured" South Africans are known to discuss their dilemma by saying, "we were not white enough under apartheid, and we are not black enough under the ANC ( ___E:African National Congress U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_National_Congress)___ )".

In 2008, the High Court in South Africa ruled that ___E:Chinese South Africans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chinese_South_Africans)___ who were residents during the apartheid era (and their descendants) are to be reclassified as "Black people", solely for the purposes of accessing affirmative action benefits, because they were also "disadvantaged" by racial discrimination.
Chinese people who arrived in the country after the end of apartheid do not qualify for such benefits.
Other than by appearance, "Coloureds" can usually be distinguished from "Blacks" by language.

Most speak ___E:Afrikaans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afrikaans)___ or English as a ___E:first language U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_language)___ , as opposed to ___E:Bantu languages U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantu_languages)___ such as ___E:Zulu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zulu_language)___ or ___E:Xhosa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Xhosa_language)___ .
They also tend to have more European-sounding names than ___E:Bantu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantu_peoples)___ names.

" ___E:Afro-Asians U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Asians)___ " or "African-Asians" are persons of mixed sub-Saharan African and ___E:Asian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asian_people)___ ancestry.
In the United States, they are also called "black Asians" or "Blasians".
Historically, Afro-Asian populations have been marginalized as a result of human migration and social conflict.

In the medieval Arab world, the ethnic designation of "Black" encompassed not only ___E:Zanj U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zanj)___ , or Africans, but also communities like ___E:Zutt U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zutt)___ , Sindis and Indians from the ___E:Indian subcontinent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indian_subcontinent)___ .

Historians estimate that between the advent of ___E:Islam U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Islam)___ in 650 CE and the abolition of slavery in the ___E:Arabian Peninsula U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arabian_Peninsula)___ in the mid-20th century, 10 to 18 million black Africans (known as the Zanj) were enslaved by ___E:east African slave traders U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_African_slave_trade)___ and transported to the Arabian Peninsula and neighboring countries.

This number far exceeded the number of slaves who were taken to the Americas.  ___E:Slavery in Saudi Arabia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_Saudi_Arabia)___ and ___E:slavery in Yemen U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_Yemen)___ was abolished in 1962, ___E:slavery in Dubai U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_Dubai)___ in 1963, and ___E:slavery in Oman U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_Oman)___ in 1970.

Several factors affected the visibility of descendants of this diaspora in 21st-century Arab societies: The traders shipped more female slaves than males, as there was a demand for them to serve as ___E:concubines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Concubinage_in_Islam)___ in harems in the Arabian Peninsula and neighboring countries.
Male slaves were castrated in order to serve as ___E:harem U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harem)___ guards.

The death toll of black African slaves from forced labor was high. The mixed-race children of female slaves and Arab owners were assimilated into the Arab owners' families under the ___E:patrilineal U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrilineal)___ ___E:kinship system U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kinship_system)___ .
As a result, few distinctive Afro-Arab communities have survived in the Arabian Peninsula and neighboring countries.

Distinctive and self-identified black communities have been reported in countries such as Iraq, with a reported 1.2 million black people ( ___E:Afro-Iraqis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Iraqis)___ ), and they attest to a history of discrimination.
These descendants of the Zanj have sought minority status from the government, which would reserve some seats in Parliament for representatives of their population.
According to Alamin M. Mazrui et al., generally in the Arabian Peninsula and neighboring countries, most of these communities identify as both black and Arab.

Afro-Iranians are people of black African ancestry residing in Iran. During the ___E:Qajar dynasty U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qajar_dynasty)___ , many wealthy households imported black African women and children as slaves to perform domestic work. This slave labor was drawn exclusively from the Zanj, who were ___E:Bantu U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantu_languages)___ -speaking peoples that lived along the ___E:African Great Lakes U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Great_Lakes)___ , in an area roughly comprising modern-day ___E:Tanzania U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tanzania)___ , ___E:Mozambique U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mozambique)___ and ___E:Malawi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malawi)___ .
About 150,000 East African and black people live in ___E:Israel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Israel)___ , amounting to just over 2% of the nation's population.

The vast majority of these, some 120,000, are ___E:Beta Israel U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beta_Israel)___ ,  most of whom are recent immigrants who came during the 1980s and 1990s from ___E:Ethiopia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopia)___ .

In addition, Israel is home to more than 5,000 members of the ___E:African Hebrew Israelites of Jerusalem U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Hebrew_Israelites_of_Jerusalem)___ movement that are ancestry of ___E:African Americans U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Americans)___ who emigrated to Israel in the 20th century, and who reside mainly in a distinct neighborhood in the ___E:Negev U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negev)___ town of ___E:Dimona U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dimona)___ .
Unknown numbers of black converts to Judaism reside in Israel, most of them converts from the United Kingdom, Canada, and the United States.
Additionally, there are around 60,000 non-Jewish African immigrants in Israel, some of whom have sought asylum.

Most of the migrants are from communities in ___E:Sudan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sudan)___ and ___E:Eritrea U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eritrea)___ , particularly the ___E:Niger-Congo U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Niger-Congo_languages)___ -speaking ___E:Nuba U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuba_peoples)___ groups of the southern ___E:Nuba Mountains U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nuba_Mountains)___ ; some are illegal immigrants.

Beginning several centuries ago, during the period of the ___E:Ottoman Empire U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ottoman_Empire)___ , tens of thousands of ___E:Zanj U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zanj)___ captives were brought by slave traders to plantations and agricultural areas situated between ___E:Antalya U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antalya_Province)___ and ___E:Istanbul U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul)___ , which gave rise to the ___E:Afro-Turk U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Afro-Turks)___ population in present-day ___E:Turkey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turkey)___ .
Some of their ancestry remained in situ , and many migrated to larger cities and towns.

Other black slaves were transported to ___E:Crete U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crete)___ , from where they or their descendants later reached the ___E:İzmir U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/%C4%B0zmir)___ area through the ___E:population exchange between Greece and Turkey U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Population_exchange_between_Greece_and_Turkey)___ in 1923, or indirectly from ___E:Ayvalık U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ayval%C4%B1k)___ in pursuit of work.
Apart from the historical Afro-Turk presence Turkey also hosts a sizeable immigrant black population since the end of the 1990s.
The community is composed mostly of modern immigrants from Ghana, Ethiopia, DRC, Sudan, Nigeria, Kenya, Eritrea, Somalia and Senegal.
According to official figures 1.5 million Africans live in Turkey and around 25% of them are located in ___E:Istanbul U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istanbul)___ .

Other studies state the majority of Africans in Turkey lives in Istanbul and report ___E:Tarlabaşı U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tarlaba%C5%9F%C4%B1)___ , ___E:Dolapdere U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolapdere)___ , ___E:Kumkapı U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumkap%C4%B1)___ , ___E:Yenikapı U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Yenikap%C4%B1)___ and ___E:Kurtuluş U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kurtulu%C5%9F)___ as having a strong African presence.
Most of the African immigrants in Turkey come to Turkey to further migrate to Europe.
Immigrants from Eastern Africa are usually refugees, meanwhile Western and Central African immigration is reported to be economically driven.

It is reported that African immigrants in Turkey regularly face economic and social challenges, notably ___E:racism U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racism_in_Turkey)___ and ___E:opposition to immigration U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opposition_to_immigration)___ by locals.

The ___E:Siddi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siddi)___ are an ethnic group inhabiting ___E:India U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/India)___ and ___E:Pakistan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan)___ .
Members are descended from the ___E:Bantu peoples U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bantu_peoples)___ of ___E:Southeast Africa U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Africa)___ .
Some were merchants, sailors, ___E:indentured servants U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indentured_servitude)___ , slaves or mercenaries.

The Siddi population is currently estimated at 270,000–350,000 individuals, living mostly in ___E:Karnataka U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karnataka)___ , ___E:Gujarat U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gujarat)___ , and ___E:Hyderabad U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hyderabad)___ in India and ___E:Makran U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makran)___ and ___E:Karachi U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Karachi)___ in Pakistan.

In the ___E:Makran U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Makran)___ strip of the ___E:Sindh U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sindh)___ and ___E:Balochistan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Balochistan,_Pakistan)___ provinces in southwestern ___E:Pakistan U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pakistan)___ , these Bantu descendants are known as the Makrani.
There was a brief "Black Power" movement in Sindh in the 1960s and many Siddi are proud of and celebrate their African ancestry.

___E:Negritos U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Negrito)___ , are a collection of various, often unrelated peoples, who were once considered a single distinct population of closely related groups, but genetic studies showed that they descended from the same ancient ___E:East Eurasian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genetic_history_of_East_Asians)___ meta-population which gave rise to modern ___E:East Asian peoples U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Asian_peoples)___ , and consist of several separate groups, as well as displaying genetic heterogeneity.

They inhabit isolated parts of ___E:Southeast Asia U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southeast_Asia)___ , and are now confined primarily to Southern Thailand,  the Malay Peninsula, and the Andaman Islands of India.

Negrito means "little black people" in ___E:Spanish U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_language)___ (negrito is the Spanish diminutive of negro, i.e., "little black person"); it is what the Spaniards called the aborigines that they encountered in the ___E:Philippines U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philippines)___ .

The term Negrito itself has come under criticism in countries like Malaysia, where it is now interchangeable with the more acceptable ___E:Semang U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Semang)___ ,  although this term actually refers to a specific group.
They have dark skin, often curly-hair and Asiatic facial characteristics, and are stockily built.
Negritos in the Philippines frequently face discrimination.
Because of their traditional hunter-gatherer lifestyle, they are marginalized and live in poverty, unable to find employment.
While census collection of ethnic background is illegal in ___E:France U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France)___ , it is estimated that there are about 2.5 – 5 million black people residing there.

From the late 19th century, the South used a ___E:colloquial U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colloquial)___ term, the one-drop rule , to classify as black a person of any known African ancestry.
This practice of ___E:hypodescent U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hypodescent)___ was not put into law until the early 20th century.

Outside of the United States, some other countries have adopted the one-drop rule, but the definition of who is black and the extent to which the one-drop "rule" applies varies greatly from country to country.

The one-drop rule may have originated as a means of increasing the number of black slaves  and was maintained as an attempt to keep the white race "pure".  [unreliable source] One of the results of the one-drop rule was the uniting of the African-American community.

Some of the most prominent abolitionists and civil-rights activists of the 19th century were multiracial, such as ___E:Frederick Douglass U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frederick_Douglass)___ , ___E:Robert Purvis U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Robert_Purvis)___ and James Mercer Langston.

Of these, 11.5 million of those shipped to ___E:South America U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_America)___ and the ___E:Caribbean U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean)___ .

Brazil was the largest importer in the Americas, with 5.5 million African slaves imported, followed by the British Caribbean with 2.76 million, the Spanish Caribbean and Spanish Mainland with 1.59 million Africans, and the French Caribbean with 1.32 million.
Today their descendants number approximately 150 million in South America and the Caribbean.
In addition to skin color, other physical characteristics such as facial features and hair texture are often variously used in classifying peoples as black in South America and the Caribbean.

In South America and the Caribbean, classification as black is also closely tied to social status and socioeconomic variables, especially in light of social conceptions of " ___E:blanqueamiento U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blanqueamiento)___ " (racial whitening) and related concepts.
The concept of race in ___E:Brazil U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brazil)___ is complex.

A Brazilian child was never automatically identified with the racial type of one or both of their parents, nor were there only two categories to choose from. Between an individual of unmixed West African ancestry and a very light ___E:mulatto U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mulatto)___ individual, more than a dozen racial categories were acknowledged, based on various combinations of ___E:hair color U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_hair_color)___ , ___E:hair texture U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hair#Texture)___ , ___E:eye color U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eye_color)___ , and ___E:skin color U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Human_skin_color)___ .
These types grade into each other like the colors of the spectrum, and no one category stands significantly isolated from the rest. In Brazil, people are classified by appearance, not heredity.
Scholars disagree over the effects of social status on racial classifications in Brazil.

It is generally believed that achieving ___E:upward mobility U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Social_mobility)___ and education results in individuals being classified as a category of lighter skin. The popular claim is that in Brazil, poor whites are considered black and wealthy blacks are considered white.

Some scholars disagree, arguing that " ___E:whitening U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_whitening)___ " of one's social status may be open to people of ___E:mixed race U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_race)___ , a large part of the population known as pardo , but a person perceived as preto (black) will continue to be classified as black regardless of wealth or social status.
From the years 1500 to 1850, an estimated 3.5 million captives were forcibly shipped from West/Central Africa to Brazil.
The territory received the highest number of slaves of any country in the Americas.
Scholars estimate that more than half of the Brazilian population is at least in part descended from these individuals.
Brazil has the largest population of Afro-ancestry outside Africa.

In contrast to the US, during the slavery period and after, the Portuguese colonial government in Brazil and the later Brazilian government did not pass formal anti- ___E:miscegenation U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Miscegenation)___ or segregation laws. As in other Latin American countries, ___E:intermarriage U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interracial_marriage)___ was prevalent during the colonial period and continued afterward.
In addition, people of ___E:mixed race U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_race)___ ( pardo ) often tended to marry white spouses, and their descendants became accepted as white.
As a result, some of the European descended population also has West African or Amerindian blood.

According to the last census of the 20th century, in which Brazilians could choose from five color/ethnic categories with which they identified, 54% of individuals identified as white, 6.2% identified as black, and 39.5% identified as pardo (brown)—a broad multi-racial category, including tri-racial persons.

In the 19th century, a philosophy of ___E:racial whitening U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_whitening)___ emerged in Brazil, related to the assimilation of mixed-race people into the white population through intermarriage.

Until recently the government did not keep data on race. However, statisticians estimate that in 1835, roughly 50% of the population was preto (black; most were ___E:enslaved U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slavery_in_Latin_America)___ ), a further 20% was pardo (brown), and 25% white, with the remainder ___E:Amerindian U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amerindian)___ .
Some classified as pardo were tri-racial.

By the 2000 census, demographic changes including the end to slavery, immigration from Europe and Asia, assimilation of multiracial persons, and other factors resulted in a population in which 6.2% of the population identified as black, 40% as pardo, and 55% as white.
Essentially most of the black population was absorbed into the multi-racial category by intermixing.
A 2007 genetic study found that at least 29% of the middle-class, white Brazilian population had some recent (since 1822 and the end of the colonial period) African ancestry.

According to the 2022 census, 10.2% of Brazilians said they were black, compared with 7.6% in 2010, and 45.3% said they were racially mixed, up from 43.1%, while the proportion of self-declared white Brazilians has fallen from 47.7% to 43.5%.
Activists from Brazil's Black movement attribute the racial shift in the population to a growing sense of pride among African-descended Brazilians in recognising and celebrating their ancestry.
The philosophy of the ___E:racial democracy U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Racial_democracy)___ in Brazil has drawn some criticism, based on economic issues.
Brazil has one of the largest gaps in income distribution in the world.
The richest 10% of the population earn 28 times the average income of the bottom 40%.
The richest 10 percent is almost exclusively white or predominantly European in ancestry.

One-third of the population lives under the ___E:poverty line U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Poverty_threshold)___ , with blacks and other ___E:people of color U:(https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/People_of_color)___ accounting for 70 percent of the poor.

Other social factors, such as illiteracy and education levels, show the same patterns of disadvantage for people of color.
